newsitem.title: BULGARIA: C.BANKER SAYS BULGARIA TO SEEK NEW RATING AT END-97.
newsitem.headline: C.BANKER SAYS BULGARIA TO SEEK NEW RATING AT END-97.

text.p: Bulgaria stands to get a better credit rating if it is sought at the end of the year, when the government has completed reforms agreed with multilateral lenders, central bank governor Svetoslav Gavriiski said.

"The end of the year is a favourable moment for Bulgaria to seek a new credit rating after fulfilling the requirements agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank," Gavriiski told reporters on Tuesday.

The new rating will reflect the newly acquired stability in Bulgaria's economy after introducing an IMF-prescribed self-regulating fixed exchange rate mechanism known as a currency board two weeks ago, he added.
The credit rating is as part of plans to launch a Eurobond issue on global markets next year to help fund huge domestic debt payments.
"We need to consider carefully our funding needs and to evaluate the debt burden on future budgets. This will be done when the 1998 budget is prepared before the end of the year," said Gavriiski.
The government has met with leading international investment banks who have offered to underwrite the issue.

Borrowing on external markets to service a three trillion lev ($1.8 billion) domestic debt and fund a restrictive budget is an option being considered by the government, which took office two months ago.

Moody's Investors Service, which last year assigned a B3 rating to a $5 million of Bulgarian Brady Bond issue, announced ten days ago a positive outlook for Bulgaria, saying that the election of a new reformist government and recent macroeconomic stabilisation measures have reduced the risk of imminent default.
The government's stringent monetary policy, backed by a $510 million standby agreement with the IMF since March, has led to a noticeable stabilisation.
Monthly inflation has steadily declined to 0.8 percent in June from 243 percent in February. Interest rates have come down to less than one percent monthly from 18 percent in March.

The currency board system, designed to restore confidence in the country's weak financial system, bans central bank lending to the government and commercial banks and requires levs in circulation be covered by foreign exchange reserves.
Bulgaria chose the mark as anchor currency and pegged the lev at 1,000 to the mark. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
